entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Yuan Dynasty (1271–1368 CE), established by Kublai Khan as the Chinese manifestation of the Mongol Empire, was the first foreign dynasty to conquer and rule all of China — governing the world's largest economy and most populous civilization from Beijing (Khanbaliq) for nearly a century. The Yuan period was the apex of Eurasian connectivity: Marco Polo's journey (1271-1291) traversed a Pax Mongolica that enabled safe trade from Venice to Beijing, bringing silk, spices, paper money, and gunpowder technology westward.

Kublai Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, conquered the Southern Song Dynasty in 1279 after 40 years of warfare — the final absorption completing the Mongol reunification of China. Kublai adopted Chinese administrative practices, employed Chinese officials, revived the Confucian examination system, and patronized Chinese culture while maintaining the Mongol ruling class. Yuan China had 60 million inhabitants — more than contemporary Europe — and its capital Khanbaliq (Beijing) was the world's largest city.

The Yuan's collapse came from the combination of economic mismanagement (massive paper money inflation), discriminatory ethnic policies (ranking Mongols, Central Asians, northern Chinese, and southern Chinese in descending legal status), natural disasters, and the 1331-1353 bubonic plague (Black Death spreading from Mongol trade routes to Europe). Zhu Yuanzhang, a Buddhist monk and commoner soldier, overthrew the Yuan in 1368 and founded the Ming Dynasty — one of history's most dramatic reversals of foreign rule.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Yuan Dynasty's Pax Mongolica created the first reliable Eurasian transcontinental trade network — spreading Marco Polo's revelations of Chinese civilization westward and the Black Death with catastrophic consequences, making it the dynasty that most changed the trajectory of both East and West simultaneously.
